client: I've been really struggling lately with my new job at this marketing agency. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one who came in without any real experience in the field, so I constantly feel like I'm falling behind or doing things wrong. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem feels pretty concrete — I just don't have the skills they have yet.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pressure right now — feeling like you're the only one without a roadmap while everyone around you seems confident can be really exhausting and isolating. I also notice that even as you're describing this struggle, there's a part of you that's already dismissing the value of exploring it, almost like you're bracing yourself for disappointment before we've even begun. I'm curious — when you imagine what "having the skills" would actually look like for you, what comes to mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess when I imagine "having the skills," I picture someone who can just walk into a room full of people and not immediately feel like they don't belong there. Like, someone who knows how to make small talk without it feeling like a performance, or who doesn't go home afterward and replay every awkward thing they said for hours. But honestly, even describing that feels kind of pointless, because I've felt this way for so long that I'm not sure I actually believe it's something that can change for me.
therapist: What you're describing — that exhausting loop of replaying conversations afterward, feeling like belonging is something other people just *have* — that's not a skills gap, it sounds much more like a long-held belief that you somehow don't quite fit. I notice you've said "pointless" and "I'm not sure it can change" twice now, and I'm wondering if that hopelessness itself might be worth looking at, because that kind of belief has a way of quietly closing doors before we even try them. What do you think that belief has been protecting you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I hadn't really thought about it that way — like the hopelessness being protective rather than just... accurate. I guess if I keep telling myself it can't change, then I don't have to risk trying to connect with people and then failing at it again, which honestly feels worse than just staying where I am. But saying that out loud makes me realize how much I've just been... managing the loneliness instead of actually doing anything about it.
therapist: That moment of recognition — "managing the loneliness instead of actually doing anything about it" — that took real courage to say out loud, and I could hear something shift as you said it, like the words were coming faster, maybe carrying more weight than you expected. It sounds like part of you has been quietly grieving this for a long time, even while another part worked hard to convince you it was just "the way things are." What would it feel like to let yourself want something different — not to pressure yourself to change, but just to allow the wanting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, just hearing you ask that made my chest feel tight, like I'm not sure I'm allowed to want something different. It's like if I let myself actually want real connection, real friendship, then I have to face how far away from that I actually am, and that feels scarier than just... staying numb to it. I think part of me has been telling myself the loneliness is fine, manageable, because wanting more and not getting it feels like it would hurt so much worse.
therapist: What you just described — "I'm not sure I'm allowed to want something different" — that's such a tender and important thing to notice, because that's not a fact about you, that's a rule you learned somewhere along the way to keep yourself safe from disappointment. The numbness has been doing a real job for you, protecting you from that gap between wanting and having, but it sounds like some part of you is tired of paying that price. I'm wondering — when you think about where that rule came from, that sense of not being allowed to want more, does anything come to mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it came from my mom, honestly. She worked so hard and never complained, and I always got this sense that wanting things — like, wanting more than what you had — was somehow selfish or ungrateful. So I just... stopped letting myself go there, because it felt safer than feeling like a bad person for having needs.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, almost carefully — made me feel like you've been holding that realization gently for a long time, maybe half-knowing it but not quite letting yourself look at it directly until now. There's something really poignant about a child who loved her mother so much that she quietly set aside her own needs to feel worthy of that love — that's not weakness, that's a profound act of loyalty that just came at a real cost to you. I'm curious, when you think about that younger version of you who learned to stop wanting — what do you wish she could have known?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what I wish she could have known is that needing things doesn't make you a burden, that wanting love and wanting to be seen is just... normal. But even saying that out loud feels strange, almost like I'm betraying something, like I'm criticizing my mom when really I know she was doing her best. It's easier to just keep telling myself it wasn't that bad, that I was fine, than to sit with the idea that something was actually lost.
therapist: What you just offered that younger version of yourself — "needing things doesn't make you a burden" — that's actually a profound and generous truth, and I notice it came out quietly, almost like you were saying something forbidden. Holding both things at once, that something real was lost *and* that your mom was doing her best, isn't a betrayal — it's actually one of the most honest and compassionate things you can do, for her and for yourself. What do you think it would mean for you, going forward, if you let both of those things be true at the same time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think... if I let both of those things be true, it might mean I stop waiting for some kind of verdict, like I don't have to decide whether my childhood was fine or terrible before I'm allowed to feel something about it. But honestly, that scares me a little, because I've kind of been using that unresolved question as a reason to keep people at a distance — like, "I can't really let anyone in until I figure this out." If I stop needing to figure it out first, I don't really know what excuse I have left for staying so isolated.
therapist: What you just named — that the unresolved question has been functioning as a kind of permission slip to stay safe — that's a really significant insight, and I notice you said it quickly, softly, like part of you wanted to slip it past yourself before you could take it back. It sounds like you're standing at a threshold right now, where the old reason for keeping distance is starting to lose its grip, and that's not just scary — it's also, maybe, a little bit like freedom. What would one very small step toward letting someone in actually look like for you, not perfectly, not with everything figured out — just one small, real thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I did say it quickly, didn't I. Like if I said it fast enough it wouldn't fully land. And now that you're asking me to sit with it, I feel this tightness in my chest, because part of me knows exactly what one small step would look like — maybe just texting my friend Carla back, she's reached out a few times and I've been leaving her on read — but even saying that out loud makes me want to find a reason why now isn't the right time.
therapist: You already know what the step is — it's Carla, and some part of you has probably known that for a while — and I notice that even as you're describing the tightness and the urge to delay, there's something almost like relief in finally saying her name out loud. The "now isn't the right time" thought is worth noticing, because that's the old pattern talking, the one that's kept you safe and lonely at the same time. What would you say to that part of you that wants to wait — if you knew that the right time has been quietly passing every time she reached out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That thing you said about "safe and lonely at the same time" kind of hit me harder than I expected, because that's exactly it, isn't it. I've been telling myself I'm protecting the friendship by waiting for the perfect moment, but really I think I've just been protecting myself from the possibility that she might not respond the way I hope. And yeah, there was something about saying her name out loud that felt different, like it made it real instead of just this vague guilt I carry around.
therapist: Saying her name made it real — and I think that matters more than you might realize, because you've just moved Carla from "vague guilt" to an actual person you want to be close to, and that's not a small thing. There's something quietly brave in recognizing that the wait isn't really about the perfect moment, it's about protecting yourself from hope, which is one of the most vulnerable things we can feel. I wonder — what do you imagine Carla might actually say if you texted her today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I actually laughed a little when you said "protecting yourself from hope" because it felt uncomfortably accurate. If I'm being honest, I think Carla would probably respond warmly — she was always kind — but then there's this other voice that says maybe she's moved on and doesn't really miss me the way I miss her. That gap between what I logically think she'd say and what my anxiety tells me she'd say is exactly what makes it so hard to just pick up my phone and do it.
therapist: That laugh feels important — like some part of you is almost relieved to be seen clearly, even when what's being seen is uncomfortable. What strikes me is that you already know, in your quieter, wiser self, that Carla would probably be warm — and that knowledge is actually data worth trusting, even when the anxious voice is louder. What do you think it would feel like, just an hour after sending that text, regardless of how she responds?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
